text:
Why, as I climb the hill

that fiercely separates me from you,

O pleasant dwelling, my eyes

fill with sad tears?

Could it be, alas, that I will not return

to you, beloved dwelling?

Who knows, for death

accompanies man everywhere,

and perhaps it will make of this tender farewell

an eternal farewell;

or perhaps the heavens will wish,

sweet dwelling of my childhood,

that there, when fierce time

turns my head gray,

I may come to seek in your bosom

a solitary tomb.

Then you, beloved home,

with your ceibas and palms

will give peaceful shade

to my funerary resting place.

Or perhaps the hard hand

of wretched misfortune

will make you pass from my people

into strange hands, alas,

and when I return as a pilgrim

from my wearisome journey,

I will not find in you the faces

that once, in another age, delighted me;

perhaps the impious hurricane

or time that loves ruins

will turn you into mournful ruins,

without mercy for my soul.

Ah! then may heaven grant,

if it brings me back to your bosom,

that your new possessor

or the fury of the hurricane

respect the exile's

memories of childhood.

translation.title: To Mount Eden
translation.editorial_note: The translation retains the island-specific ceiba and palm imagery and the final appeal to an exile’s childhood memories.
